concept_mcqs.stem:
You are handed yesterday's paid campaign funnel. Budget and delivery cap keep landing-page views fixed at about 210/day for the next two weeks.

```text
Step             Count   CR to next
LP views         210     45%
Form starts       95     80%
Form submits      76     —
Target: +30% leads (form submits) without changing traffic volume.
```
Which single change most likely reaches the target under the constraint above?
options: Cut form fields to raise LP→Start from 45% to 60%, keeping Start→Submit at 80%.
Add an exit-intent modal that collects 15 extra emails but does not submit the main form.
Tweak button copy to raise Start→Submit from 80% to 90%, keeping LP→Start at 45%.
Rework ad creative to raise CTR from 2.1% to 3.0%, keeping LP views at ~210/day.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Baseline leads = 210 × 0.45 × 0.80 = 75.6 (~76). Raising LP→Start to 60% yields 210 × 0.60 × 0.80 = 100.8 (~101), which exceeds +30% (target ≈ 99). Improving only Start→Submit to 90% yields 85 (short). CTR changes don't matter if LP views are capped at ~210/day. Capturing extra emails outside the defined "lead" (form submits) does not move the primary KPI.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B is tempting because improving the final step feels high leverage, but 210 × 0.45 × 0.90 = 85 is insufficient. C sounds right generally, but the stem fixes LP views, making CTR irrelevant short term. D feels like micro-conversion capture, but the success definition is form submits; side-collection won't count.

options: Correct conversion counts but misattributed to Direct/None.
Zero recorded conversions despite successful form submissions.
Roughly double-counted conversions on every submit.
Conversions recorded only on mobile due to event name length limits.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The custom event name in the trigger (lead_submit) does not match the event in the tracking plan (lead_submitted). The conversion tag never fires, so conversions report 0.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B would require the tag to fire twice, but here it fires zero times. C attribution issues don't apply when no conversion event fires at all. D device-specific limits are not implicated; the mismatch is purely a name mismatch.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A developer implements form tracking like this:

```html
<form id="lead" action="/thank-you" method="POST" onsubmit="trackThenGo(event)">
  <input name="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Get demo</button>
</form>
<script>
function trackThenGo(e){
  e.preventDefault();
  dataLayer.push({event:"lead_submitted"});
  window.location.href = "/thank-you"; // immediate navigation
}
</script>
```
Which change most reliably ensures the conversion event is captured before the redirect?
options: Add `async` to the script tag so it runs faster before redirect.
Mark the submit event as non-interaction to reduce bounce rate inflation.
Fire a duplicate page_view on the thank-you page instead of the submit event.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Using an event callback (or equivalent tag hitCallback) holds the navigation until the beacon is dispatched, preventing the redirect from aborting the request.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B logs pageviews, not the defined conversion, and still risks missing the submit if the redirect is immediate. C is about bounce rate semantics, not delivery reliability. D `async` affects parsing but not ensuring network send before navigation.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A landing page A/B test returns:

```text
Intended split: 50/50
Observed over 7 days:
Variant A: 1,200 sessions, 96 submits
Variant B:   800 sessions, 80 submits
Primary KPI: submit rate
```
What is the best next step before declaring a winner?
options: Investigate sample ratio mismatch (SRM) and traffic filters/allocation before interpreting lift.
Declare B the winner because 10% > 8% regardless of sample split.
Extend the test until both variants have exactly equal sessions, then declare a winner.
Weight B's conversion rate up by 50% to adjust for fewer sessions and decide now.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A large, unexpected 60/40 split suggests SRM or allocation issues. Diagnose (allocation bugs, targeting differences, bot filters) before trusting the observed lift.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B ignores potential bias from SRM. C equal counts are unnecessary and can waste time; what's needed is to fix allocation bias. D ad-hoc weighting is statistically unsound without fixing the underlying issue.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Extract from a draft campaign brief:

```markdown
Business goal: Grow pipeline.
Marketing objective (Q3): Increase qualified demo bookings by 25%.
Proposed primary KPI: Landing page CTR from ads.
Secondary KPIs: Time on page, scroll depth.
```
What should be the primary KPI to align with the stated objective?
options: Landing page click-through rate (CTR)
Number of qualified demo bookings
Average scroll depth on the landing page
Form start rate (visits → starts)
concept_mcqs.explanation: The objective is to increase qualified demo bookings; the primary KPI must directly measure that outcome (count or rate of qualified demo bookings).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B and C are upstream engagement proxies and can improve without affecting bookings. D is closer to the funnel but still a micro-step and can rise while bookings stagnate if start→submit or qualification drops.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A shortened URL is used in ads:

```text
Ad URL: https://sho.rt/try?utm_source=meta&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=spring
Redirects:
1) https://sho.rt/try?...  → 301 → https://brand.com/go
2) https://brand.com/go    → 302 → https://brand.com/landing
```
Analytics is configured to attribute by UTM parameters on the landing URL. What is the most likely attribution outcome?
options: All traffic is bucketed under Referral from sho.rt.
UTM campaign is preserved because 301s forward the query string by default.
UTMs are recovered from the ad platform API during import so reports remain accurate.
Most visits appear as Direct/None on the landing page.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The first hop drops the UTM query string when redirecting to `/go`. Without UTMs on the final URL, analytics cannot attribute and typically classifies the visit as Direct/None.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B 301s do not automatically append missing query strings. C referrer may be present, but the question specifies attribution configured by UTMs; without them, default often becomes Direct. D API imports don't reconstruct missing per-click UTMs unless an auto-tagging integration is in place, which is not stated.

options: Comparing conversion rates between the two forms on the same page
Attributing submissions by marketing channel
Counting total submissions sitewide
Measuring device breakdown of conversions
concept_mcqs.explanation: Without `form_id`, events from both forms are indistinguishable on the same URL, preventing per-form funnel and conversion rate comparisons.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B channel attribution relies on UTMs/referrer, not `form_id`. C total submissions can still be counted. D device breakdown comes from user agent, not `form_id`.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your hero section CSS keeps the form below the fold on most laptops: ```html

All-in-one Freight Quotes

Instant quotes. No surprises.

Get a demo
... the lead form ...
``` ```css .hero { height: 100vh; display:flex; align-items:center; } ``` LP→Start is 45% with a 70% scroll drop at 600px. Which minimal change is most likely to improve LP→Start?
options: Change button color from blue to green for higher contrast.
Add testimonials below the fold under the form.
Add an exit-intent popup offering a 10% discount code.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Exposing the form without scrolling directly addresses the observed scroll drop-off and should increase form starts. The other changes do not address the above-the-fold visibility constraint.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B can capture abandoning users but doesn't fix the main bottleneck. C social proof helps nearer to the form but not if it's unseen. D color tweaks are minor compared to moving critical UI into view.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your KPI plan reads:

```yaml
objective: Acquire 500 leads in Q2 at CPL <= $40
primary_kpis:
  - sessions
  - bounce_rate
  - avg_time_on_page
  - lp_to_form_start_rate
secondary_kpis:
  - nps
```
Which KPI is missing to validate the objective as written?
options: Click-through rate (CTR) from ads to landing page
Newsletter subscriptions captured via popup
Cost per lead (CPL) based on media spend and valid submissions
Average order value (AOV) from ecommerce
concept_mcqs.explanation: The objective includes a cost constraint. You must track CPL using spend and valid lead counts to validate success.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B helps diagnose traffic but doesn't validate cost efficiency. C is a different conversion. D is unrelated to a lead-gen objective.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Mid-campaign, the team switches the primary KPI from `form_submits` to `form_starts` to "get faster signal". A week later:

```text
Before switch (Week 3):  95 starts, 76 submits
After switch  (Week 4): 145 starts, 78 submits
Budget unchanged; traffic sources shifted toward broader audiences.
```
What most likely happened to the funnel and risk to the objective?
options: Both steps improved; the objective is now safer because starts rose significantly.
Optimizing to starts increased LP→Start but worsened Start→Submit, so leads barely moved and risk to the objective increased.
Start volumes grew and will mechanically convert to more submits next week without further action.
Nothing material changed; start counts are noisy and do not affect submits.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Shifting optimization to an upstream event often brings lower-intent visitors who start more forms but finish fewer, depressing Start→Submit. With similar submits, the objective (leads) is at greater risk despite higher starts.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B contradicts the flat submit count. C ignores a systematic optimization change. D assumes a lag that isn't evidenced; for simple lead forms, most submits occur same-session.

scenario_questions.scenario:
You receive this rough campaign brief for a B2B SaaS freight platform targeting mid-market shippers:

```markdown
Goal: Grow pipeline.
Audience: Logistics managers.
Offer: Book a demo.
Timing: Q3.
Budget: $60k.
Notes: Our brand is premium. We think Europe will work.
```
Performance to date (last quarter): 12,000 LP sessions, 3.8% form start rate, 80% start→submit, 25% demo qualification rate (sales-accepted), $52 CPL, 720 total leads, 180 qualified demos.
scenario_questions.task: Rewrite the objective as 2–3 SMART statements aligned to funnel stage and positioning, pick a primary KPI for each, and justify audience and geo choices. Include realistic targets using the baseline metrics and budget. State what you will not optimize for this quarter and why.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Three SMART objectives, for example: 1) Increase qualified demo bookings by 30% in Q3 (from 180 to 234) at CPL ≤ $45 by improving LP→Start from 3.8% to 6% through above-the-fold form placement and reducing fields from 8 to 5. Primary KPI: number of qualified demos; guardrail: CPL. 2) Improve Start→Submit from 80% to 88% by removing phone requirement and clarifying privacy copy. Primary KPI: submit rate; guardrail: lead acceptance rate. 3) Maintain EU market test to DE/FR/NL only (English + localized hero) targeting companies shipping 500–5,000 consignments/month; do not expand to Southern Europe this quarter due to limited localization and higher CAC. Audience justification references ICP fit (mid-market logistics managers) and positioning (premium, reliability). Clearly calls out deprioritized metrics (e.g., time on page) and channels not in scope. Targets numerically link baseline volumes to end outcomes under fixed budget, with a simple math check that 12,000 sessions × 6% × 88% × 25% ≈ 158 qualified demos per 12k sessions and a plan to add traffic or efficiency to reach 234 total.

rubric.criterion: SMART objectives stated with baselines, numeric targets, and time bounds
Primary KPI and guardrails chosen per objective with rationale
Audience and geo justified using positioning and funnel logic; clear out-of-scope callouts
Targets are internally consistent (math linking funnel steps and budget)

scenario_questions.scenario:
You control the landing page. Current week metrics by device:

```text
Device     Sessions  LP→Start  Start→Submit
Desktop      6,000     5.2%       85%
Mobile       9,000     2.1%       72%
```
Form has 8 fields including phone (required) and company size (dropdown with 12 options). Scroll heatmaps show 68% drop before the form on mobile. Sales rejects 28% of mobile leads as unresponsive within 7 days.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a prioritized, two-sprint CRO plan (max 5 items) that can ship in 4 weeks. For each item, state expected impact on a specific funnel step and estimate incremental qualified leads per week, showing assumptions. Include at least one holdout or A/B design to validate impact and a guardrail for lead quality.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A backlog such as: 1) Reduce hero height and place form above the fold on mobile (expect mobile LP→Start from 2.1%→3.8%). 9,000 × (3.8%-2.1%) × 72% × (1-0.28 reject) ≈ +89 qualified leads/week. Validate via A/B with SRM check; guardrail: rejection rate must not rise. 2) Remove phone as required; move to optional with progressive disclosure (expect Start→Submit +6pp on both devices, quality guardrail: phone capture rate ≥40% via step-2). 15,000 sessions × 5.2% weighted start rate × +6pp submit ≈ +47 leads/week net; monitor rejection rate. 3) Simplify company size to 5 buckets (reduce friction; predict +1pp LP→Start and +2pp Start→Submit mobile). 4) Add inline error copy and real-time validation to cut abandonments at email step (+2pp Start→Submit). 5) Add trust badges near the submit button on mobile (smaller, +0.5pp Start→Submit). Each item ties to a test design and guardrails (lead acceptance ≥75%, CPL stable).

rubric.criterion: Prioritized actions mapped to specific funnel steps with plausible rationale
Back-of-envelope impact estimates shown with assumptions and math
Includes an A/B or holdout design and SRM/guardrail considerations
Addresses lead quality explicitly (e.g., rejection rate)

scenario_questions.task: Identify at least three concrete defects or risks that will cause mismeasurement of the primary KPI (form submits) and propose precise fixes. Describe a QA checklist (5–7 steps) you would run to validate end-to-end data quality from UTMs to CRM.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Issues and fixes: 1) Event name mismatch (`form_submitted` vs `form_submit`) causes zero conversions; align to `form_submitted` or update mapping. 2) Missing required properties in the push; include `form_id`, `page_url`, `utm_source`, `email` at submit (pass via hidden fields or read from state). 3) Redirect/Meta refresh after 0.2s can abort network beacons; delay with hitCallback or increase refresh to ≥2s and send hits on submit and TYP load. 4) Only `submit` listener; no `form_started` event captured—add focus/change listener to first input or CTA click to measure starts. 5) Risk that UTMs are dropped via internal redirect; ensure `/thank-you` preserves UTMs in session storage or rely on session-scoped acquisition. QA checklist: verify UTM persistence through redirects; test both forms with known test UTMs; confirm events in debug view with correct names and properties; validate one submit flows into analytics conversions and CRM with correct source; check deduplication (no double fires on TYP + submit); run device/browser matrix; confirm timeouts/callbacks fire before navigation.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies at least three concrete defects tied to the artefacts
Proposes precise, technically sound fixes for each defect
QA checklist covers UTMs→events→conversions→CRM with clear steps

scenario_questions.scenario:
Two-week LP headline test summary:

```text
Allocation: intended 50/50; observed 58/42 (A/B)
Traffic mix shift mid-test: +30% mobile on B after day 5
Results: A — 2,340 sessions, 187 submits; B — 1,690 sessions, 183 submits
Guardrails: lead acceptance rate (A: 76%, B: 69%), CPL target ≤ $45 (A: $47, B: $44)
```
Stakeholders want to ship B because CPL is lower and submits are similar.
scenario_questions.task: Decide whether to ship B now, keep testing, or revert. Justify with reference to allocation bias, device mix, primary vs guardrail KPIs, and next steps to reach a confident decision. Propose at least two test design fixes for a rerun.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Recommendation: Do not ship B yet. Although CPL is $1 lower, B shows a materially lower lead acceptance rate (69% vs 76%) and suffered allocation/device mix shifts (58/42 split; +30% mobile to B) that likely depress conversion. Primary KPI (submit rate) does not clearly favor B (A: 8.0%, B: 10.8% if naive, but given mix and acceptance drop, net qualified demos are similar or worse). Next steps: investigate SRM causes (allocation bug, audience targeting filter, bot filters); stratify by device and compute qualified submit rate; enforce allocation control and device balancing in the experiment platform; rerun with equalized traffic, pre-registered analysis plan, and minimum sample size to detect a defined MDE; keep guardrails (acceptance ≥75%, CPL ≤$45). Test design fixes: block randomization by device, disable mid-test targeting changes, and use conversion event = qualified submit rather than raw submit.

rubric.criterion: Clear go/hold/revert decision with justification anchored in primary KPI and guardrails
Correct identification of allocation/device mix biases and their impact
Actionable next steps, including experiment design fixes and analysis plan
Consideration of qualified outcome (not just raw submits)

practical_tasks.title: Produce a Campaign Brief for a Lead-Gen Push

Base targets on simple funnel math from plausible baselines.

Outlines a high-level channel and asset plan consistent with objectives
Explicitly lists 1–2 out-of-scope metrics or channels for this push

Objectives are SMART and aligned; KPIs and guardrails are well-chosen

Form specification: fields (required/optional), validation, error states, thank-you behavior, deduplication approach
Tracking plan: event names for start/submit, required properties (form_id, page_url, email, UTMs), timing/callbacks, and mapping to analytics goals
Attribution scheme: UTM parameters with examples, redirect handling, and parameter persistence plan
Initial A/B test idea with primary KPI, guardrails, allocation, and stopping criteria
QA checklist covering UTMs → events → conversions → CRM with device/browser matrix
Risk register noting at least two likely failure modes (e.g., SRM, dropped UTMs) and mitigations

rubric.criterion: Wireframe and UX choices address known bottlenecks (e.g., above-the-fold, clarity)
Form spec is complete and balances friction vs quality (fields, validation, states)
Tracking plan is precise (events, properties, callbacks) and maps to KPIs/goals
Attribution/UTM scheme and redirect handling are correct and testable
Test plan and QA checklist are actionable with guardrails and stopping rules

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your sitemap lists both the clean and a parameterized version of the same product URL. The parameterized page also sets a self-referencing canonical.

```xml
<!-- sitemap.xml extract -->
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <url><loc>https://www.example.com/red-shoes</loc></url>
  <url><loc>https://www.example.com/red-shoes?utm=aff1</loc></url>
</urlset>
```

```html
<!-- https://www.example.com/red-shoes?utm=aff1 -->
<head>
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://www.example.com/red-shoes?utm=aff1" />
  <title>Red Shoes | Example</title>
</head>
```

After recrawl, which Index Coverage status is MOST likely for the parameterized URL in Search Console?
options: Excluded by ‘noindex’
Alternate page with proper canonical tag
Indexed, not submitted in sitemap
Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user
concept_mcqs.explanation: Including both URLs in the sitemap while the parameterized page self-canonicals often leads Google to pick the clean URL as canonical anyway. Search Console typically labels the parameterized URL as “Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user.”
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: It is submitted in the sitemap, so “Indexed, not submitted” is unlikely. C: “Alternate page with proper canonical tag” appears when the canonical points to another URL, not to itself. D: There is no noindex shown; nothing suggests a noindex directive.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A thank-you page is accidentally indexed. Your current setup is:

```text
# robots.txt
User-agent: *
Disallow: /thank-you/
```

```html
<!-- https://www.example.com/thank-you/ -->
<head>
  <meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">
</head>
```

The page must remain accessible after form submission but should not appear in search. What change will most reliably remove it from the index without breaking the conversion flow?
options: Remove the robots.txt Disallow so Google can crawl and process the noindex, then keep it accessible
Keep robots.txt Disallow and wait; Google will eventually drop it
Return HTTP 410 for /thank-you/ so Google deindexes it immediately
Add it to the XML sitemap with <priority>0.0</priority> so Google de-prioritizes it
concept_mcqs.explanation: If robots.txt blocks crawl, Google cannot see the noindex tag. Allow crawling so Google can fetch the page and honor the noindex while the page remains accessible to users after submission.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Waiting won’t help because Google can’t fetch the noindex. B: Sitemap priority is ignored by Google for indexing decisions. D: 410 would remove it but also breaks the live thank-you page needed after form submission.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your Non-Brand Google Ads campaign shows the following search terms and spend for the ad group targeting "digital marketing agency":

```csv
search_term,clicks,conversions,cost_usd
"digital marketing jobs",58,0,232.10
"digital marketing agency",44,3,141.80
"digital marketing hiring near me",27,0,96.70
"marketing internship",31,0,71.20
"digital marketing services",22,2,83.40
```

You want to cut waste from employment-related queries without harming relevant “services/agency” traffic. What change is most effective?
options: Add negative broad terms at campaign level: "job", "jobs", "hiring", "internship"
Add negative phrase "digital marketing job" at campaign level
Add negative exact [digital marketing jobs] at ad group level only
Add negative broad "job" at campaign level
concept_mcqs.explanation: Single-word negative broad terms block any query containing the term. Adding the set {job, jobs, hiring, internship} at campaign level reliably strips most employment-related queries while preserving services/agency traffic.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Only “job” won’t catch plurals or synonyms; you’ll still pay for jobs, hiring, internship. C: Exact negatives block only that exact query; variants still slip through. D: Phrase negatives require the exact phrase order and miss other job-related patterns.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Account structure:

```text
Campaigns
- Brand (applies shared list: "Irrelevant Content")
  - Ad group: Brand Core (KW: [acme shoes], "acme shoes")
  - Ad group: Brand Reviews (KW: "acme shoes reviews")
- Non-Brand (applies shared list: "Irrelevant Content")
  - Ad group: Running Shoes (KW: +running +shoes)

Shared negative list: "Irrelevant Content" = { review, reviews }
```

Search term “acme shoes reviews” now gets zero impressions. Why?
options: Non-Brand campaign’s negatives are overriding Brand
Brand exact keyword lost auctions due to low bids
Phrase match in Brand doesn’t capture the plural form
The shared negative "reviews" is blocking it across all campaigns
concept_mcqs.explanation: Shared negative lists apply to every campaign they’re attached to. With “reviews” in the shared list and applied to Brand, the Brand Reviews ad group is blocked before matching can occur.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Bid issues don’t cause zero eligibility across all auctions. C: Cross-campaign negatives don’t override unless applied; here, the shared list is the culprit. D: Phrase match handles plurals; the block is from the negative.

concept_mcqs.stem:
An ad group contains these keywords:

```text
[tennis shoe]
"tennis shoes"
tennis shoes
```

For the query `tennis shoe`, which keyword will Google MOST likely match?
options: [tennis shoe]
"tennis shoes"
tennis shoes
Whichever keyword has the higher Quality Score at auction time
concept_mcqs.explanation: Google prefers the most specific match type when available within the same ad group. The exact match [tennis shoe] is the closest match to the query `tennis shoe`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Phrase could match, but exact takes precedence when available in the same ad group. C: Broad could match, but it’s less specific. D: Ad Rank/QS can break ties, but the hierarchy favors exact within the same ad group.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You pin RSA components as follows:

```text
Headlines (pinned)
1: Buy Running Shoes Online (Pin H1)
2: Official ACME Store (Pin H2)
3: Free Shipping Over $50 (Pin H3)

10 additional headlines: Unpinned (eligible only for H4+)
Descriptions: 4 total, none pinned
```

Compared with an otherwise identical RSA with no pinning, what outcome is most likely over time?
options: Higher ad strength and CTR due to consistent branding
Higher Quality Score because more headlines are provided
Lower ad strength and fewer combinations, risking lower CTR/ad relevance in some auctions
No impact; pinning only changes the preview, not delivery
concept_mcqs.explanation: Pinning constrains combinations, often reducing ad strength and limiting adaptation to different queries/contexts, which can hurt CTR and ad relevance in some auctions.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Consistency can help brand safety, but ad strength typically drops with heavy pinning. C: Pinning affects which combinations can serve. D: QS won’t rise just because more assets exist; how they serve matters.

concept_mcqs.stem:
After improving page speed for your main ads’ landing page, metrics changed as follows:

```text
Core Web Vitals (lab)    Before    After
LCP                       4.5 s     2.2 s
INP                       400 ms    180 ms
CLS                       0.20      0.10

Google Ads (component)   Before    After
Landing page exp.        Average   (expected) Above average
Quality Score            5/10      (expected) ?
Avg CPC at same bids     $1.80     (expected) ?
```

Assuming creatives and bids are unchanged, what is the most likely effect on QS and CPC?
options: CPC drops by ~50% immediately
QS improves; CPC falls slightly due to better landing page experience
QS unchanged; CPC rises due to competition
No change in QS or CPC; CWV is not used in Ads
concept_mcqs.explanation: Improved landing page experience feeds into Quality Score. With higher QS at the same bids, you need less CPC to maintain Ad Rank, so average CPC typically falls modestly, not by half.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Better landing page experience raises QS, not keeps it flat. C: Landing page experience is a QS component. D: The effect is real but not that dramatic in most cases.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your sitemap includes URLs that now 301 to consolidated pages.

```xml
<url>
  <loc>https://www.example.com/mens/sale</loc>
  <lastmod>2026-01-10</lastmod>
</url>
```

```http
GET /mens/sale  HTTP/2
HTTP/2 301
Location: https://www.example.com/sale
```

In Search Console’s Pages (Indexing) report, what status is most likely for the submitted redirecting URL?
options: Excluded by ‘noindex’
Submitted URL seems to be a redirect
Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user
Alternate page with proper canonical tag
concept_mcqs.explanation: When a sitemap includes a URL that redirects, Search Console reports “Submitted URL seems to be a redirect.”
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/C: These are canonicalization states, not redirects. D: There is no noindex directive involved.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You added this negative keyword to an ad group:

```text
[red shoes]
```

The search term report still shows spend on `red shoes sale`. Why?
options: Close variants override negatives if intent seems similar
Phrase negatives are required for exact-match negatives to work
Exact-match negatives only block the exact term (or very close variants), not longer queries containing it
Broad-match keywords ignore negatives at serve time
concept_mcqs.explanation: Negative exact only blocks the exact term or its very close variants. Adding words like “sale” makes it a different query that remains eligible unless you use a phrase/broad negative covering that pattern.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Negatives don’t yield to close variants. C: Exact negatives work, but only for the exact term. D: Negatives always apply; broad keywords don’t ignore them.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You add a campaign-level negative BROAD match:

```text
red shoes
```

Which query will still be eligible to trigger your ads, assuming no other negatives apply?
options: cheap red shoes
red shoe
shoes red on sale
red running shoes
concept_mcqs.explanation: Negative broad requires all the negative terms to be present, in any order, as the same words. “red shoe” lacks the plural “shoes”, and negatives don’t match close variants, so it slips through.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/B/D: Each contains both “red” and “shoes” (regardless of order) and will be blocked by a broad-match negative comprising those two words.

scenario_questions.scenario: A category on your ecommerce site (/running-shoes/) has flat organic clicks for two months despite ongoing link acquisition. In Search Console you see a rising count of “Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user” for URLs like /running-shoes?color=red and /running-shoes?sort=price. The sitemap currently lists faceted URLs. Robots.txt does not block these parameters. Some faceted pages self-canonical to themselves; others point to /running-shoes/.
scenario_questions.task: Diagnose the core cause and propose a prioritized plan to restore healthy indexing and traffic. Specify exactly which changes you would make to canonical tags, sitemaps, parameter handling, internal links, and any Search Console actions. Justify why your ordering addresses the root cause fastest with least risk.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Root cause: mixed and conflicting canonicalization plus sitemap pollution with parameterized/faceted URLs. Google is picking its own canonicals, causing index bloat and dilution. Plan: 1) Standardize canonical tags so all parameterized/faceted variants canonical to the clean category URL, never to themselves. 2) Remove all parameterized URLs from the XML sitemap; keep only canonical, indexable URLs. 3) In templates, add rel="prev/next" is deprecated, so instead ensure clear pagination linking and consistent canonical to page 1 or to self by page; avoid parameter canonicals. 4) If certain facets merit indexing (e.g., /running-shoes/red/ as a static path), create static, crawlable URLs with unique content and self-referencing canonicals; otherwise keep facets non-indexable via meta robots noindex,follow while allowing crawl (do NOT robots.txt disallow if you rely on noindex). 5) Ensure internal links point to canonical URLs only (nav, filters). 6) Clean sitemap and resubmit in Search Console; use the URL Inspection tool on representative examples to confirm canonical selection. 7) Optionally configure parameter hints in Search Console (legacy parameter tool if available) with caution; prefer on-site signals. 8) Monitor Coverage for drops in duplicate states and Performance for recovery; do not expect immediate gains—allow several crawls. Justification: Removing conflicting signals and sitemap noise lets Google converge on canonical pages; allowing crawl with noindex where needed avoids zombie indexing from robots.txt blocks.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies conflicting canonicals and sitemap pollution as the core cause
Gives precise canonical and sitemap corrections (parameter pages canonicalizing to clean URL; remove non-canonical URLs from sitemap)
Proposes proper handling of facets (crawl allowed; noindex where appropriate; only create indexable static facet pages when justified)
Addresses internal linking to canonical URLs and pagination signals appropriately
Details concrete Search Console actions and a monitoring plan with rationale/prioritization

scenario_questions.scenario: You must build a search campaign for a mid-sized retailer launching “TrailRun” shoes. Budget is $1,000/day. The site has good brand equity and existing category pages. Historic SQR shows many irrelevant queries around jobs and DIY shoe repairs. The client wants strong coverage of brand and non-brand with room to test messaging.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a complete account structure (campaigns, ad groups), match type strategy in the close-variant era, RSA copy approach (pinning policy), and a negative strategy (levels and shared lists). Include how you will separate brand vs non-brand and protect each with negatives. Specify your initial bidding strategy and what you will measure in week 1 to iterate.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Structure: Separate Brand and Non-Brand campaigns. Optionally split Non-Brand by intent/theme (e.g., Trail Running Shoes Generic, Men’s, Women’s). Keywords: start with exact and phrase for high-intent heads (e.g., [trail running shoes], "men's trail running shoes"), plus limited broad in tightly themed ad groups under smart bidding once negatives are in place. Keep SKAGs only where volume justifies; otherwise tight theming (2–5 KWs per ad group). RSAs: 2 per ad group, minimal pinning (only legal/brand lines pinned), use keyword variants in some headlines; include distinct value props and CTAs; test description angles. Negatives: Account-level shared lists for jobs/careers/DIY repairs (job, jobs, hiring, internship, repair, DIY, fix), applied to all non-brand campaigns; do NOT apply to Brand Reviews/Support if those ad groups are intentional. Campaign-level brand negatives ("trailrun") applied to Non-Brand to prevent bleed; add non-brand generic negatives to Brand (e.g., -cheap, -discount if unwanted). Bidding: Start with tCPA or tROAS if sufficient conversion history; otherwise Maximize Conversions with a cap, then move to tCPA once 30+ conversions collected. Week-1 measurement: impression share by segment (brand vs non-brand), search term coverage, QS components (ad relevance, landing exp), RSA asset-level performance, N-grams for new negatives, and early CPA/CVR by ad group. Iterate by adding negatives, promoting strong search terms to exact, and refining RSAs/LP alignment.

rubric.criterion: Clear separation of Brand vs Non-Brand with appropriate negative sculpting between them
Coherent ad group theming with match-type strategy suited to close variants (exact/phrase focus; cautious broad under smart bidding)
RSA policy with minimal pinning and purposeful asset diversity
Robust negative strategy (levels, shared lists) that addresses known irrelevant themes
Initial bidding strategy plus concrete week-1 measurements and iteration plan

concept_mcqs.stem:
You noticed this pattern and upcoming plan:

Last 90 days:

- IG best post time for your audience: Tue 11:00.

Next week (Week 12):
Tue 10:00 — Newsletter "Starter Guide"
Tue 11:00 — IG Carousel "Step 1–3 Teaser" (tentative)

To minimize the IG reach loss while keeping the Tuesday theme coherent with the newsletter, which scheduling change is best?

Move the IG carousel to 11:00 Tue and post a Story teaser at 09:00
Keep the IG carousel at 09:40 Tue and add a Story at 09:00 with a countdown to the email

D: Moving to Monday avoids the collision but breaks the Tuesday content theme and risks weaker performance at an unvalidated time.

Next week you plan to add 2 new creatives. Welcome email sends T+24h after signup; ~30% of purchases happen Day 2 post-click.

Pause the 4 lowest-CTR ads in A, keep top 2, and raise budget to $60/day

concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Duplicating splits learning and signals, likely prolonging instability. C: Optimizing for clicks increases volume but degrades lead quality, harming downstream email performance. D: Frequency caps do not address the core issue of dispersed conversions across too many ads.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You see this performance:

Retargeting audience (last 7 days)
- Paid social frequency: 2.8
- CPA trend: +22% WoW

Welcome sequence
Day 1 (T+0h): Open 68%, Click 5.2%, Unsub 0.3%
Day 2 (T+24h): Open 41%, Click 1.1%, Unsub 0.9%
```
You planned Day 2 at T+24h and a retargeting cap of 3. What change best reduces fatigue and CPA without heavy rework?
options: Pause Day 2 for a week and double paid social budget to offset CPA
Delay Day 2 to T+36h and lower paid social frequency cap to 2
Keep Day 2 timing and switch retargeting objective to Reach for cheaper impressions
Send Day 2 earlier at T+12h and raise cap to 4 to compress the funnel

concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Compressing increases overlap and likely raises complaints and CPA. C: Reach objective sacrifices conversion quality; impressions alone won’t fix CPA. D: Pausing an early lifecycle touch harms revenue timing and doubling budget often worsens CPA under fatigue.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You must pace a $700, 7-day paid social flight feeding a welcome series that starts immediately. History shows:

- 70% of qualified leads arrive Mon–Wed.
- Weekend CPMs are -25%, but weekend-acquired leads have -18% Day-1 open rates.
```
Which pacing plan most likely maximizes qualified leads without starving midweek entry into the series?

Spend $180 Mon, $180 Tue, $160 Wed, $80 Thu, $50 Fri, $25 Sat, $25 Sun
Spend $80 Mon–Wed, then $160/day Thu–Sun to exploit cheaper CPMs
Spend $350 Mon, $350 Tue, $0 the rest

concept_mcqs.stem: You need to send a proactive WhatsApp message to opted-in users whose last session is >24h ago. Which approved template complies with channel rules and good privacy practice for a promotional reminder?

concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Incorrect category (UTILITY) for a promotion; risks template rejection/misuse. C: Lacks any opt-out guidance, weakening privacy practice for a promo push. D: Utility content is allowed but is not the promotional reminder you intend.

options: All three surfaces (GA4 reports, BigQuery, and Ads import) count two purchases and double revenue/conversions.
BigQuery export automatically dedupes purchase events with the same `transaction_id`, so it shows one row; GA4 reports and Ads each count two.
GA4 dedupes only when the duplicates are in the same session ID, so these two count twice in reports but Ads import still dedupes to one.
GA4 standard reports count one purchase and one revenue total; BigQuery continues to show two raw rows; the Google Ads conversion import counts one conversion.
concept_mcqs.explanation: GA4 reporting deduplicates ecommerce purchases by `transaction_id` while the BigQuery export remains event-level and includes duplicates. Google Ads imports from GA4 respect GA4’s deduplication, so Ads will also count one conversion for this order ID.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Tempting if you think BigQuery logic mirrors reports; it does not — BigQuery is raw. C: GA4 deduplication uses `transaction_id`, not session ID. D: The export never auto-dedupes; deduplication happens in reporting layers, not in the raw export.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You upload non-Google cost data to GA4 using the Cost Data import with the file below. Your UTMs for this campaign use `utm_source=bing` and `utm_medium=paid`.

```csv
date,campaign,source,medium,clicks,impressions,cost,currency
2026-07-01,Brand_US_Summer,bing,cpc,2400,120000,5600,USD
```
The import succeeds. In the GA4 Advertising workspace Cost analysis, what will you see for this campaign on 2026‑07‑01?
options: Costs appear joined to sessions and conversions but attributed to Source = (not set) because campaign is the only required join key.
Nothing appears because GA4 rejects rows whose `medium` isn’t exactly `paid` for Bing.
Costs will auto-map to the Default Channel Grouping and still join because GA4 normalizes `cpc` and `paid` as the same.
Costs and clicks appear, but they won’t join to traffic: you’ll see cost and clicks with 0 sessions and 0 conversions because `medium` mismatches your UTMs.
concept_mcqs.explanation: GA4 joins imported costs to traffic using Date + Source + Medium + Campaign. Because your UTMs use `paid` but the file says `cpc`, the rows won’t join to any sessions, yielding cost with 0 sessions/conversions.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: GA4 does not reject on `medium` values; it just fails to join. C: GA4 does not normalize `cpc` to `paid`. D: The join requires Source+Medium+Campaign+Date; campaign alone is not enough, so attribution to (not set) won’t happen.

options: GA4 ignores user-defined event parameters that try to overwrite reserved attribution dimensions like session campaign.
You need to register `session_campaign` as a session-scoped custom dimension before it appears in Traffic acquisition.
The parameter is only respected when sent with `first_visit` or `session_start`, not with `page_view`.
The parameter works but requires 72 hours to backfill historical values before changing the report.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Attribution dimensions in Traffic acquisition (first user/session campaign, source, medium) are derived from GA collection logic and reserved; custom parameters cannot overwrite them.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: GA4 custom dimensions support event- or user-scope only; session scope is not available to override attribution. C: Delays don’t turn custom params into built-in dimensions. D: Even on `session_start`, you can’t override built-in attribution dimensions with arbitrary params.

options: Both GA4 and Ads stopped measuring conversions for denied users; the flat Ads number is a reporting cache artifact that will drop later.
Paid Search didn’t actually drop; with ad_storage denied, GA4 lost deterministic Ads identifiers so attribution shifted away from Paid Search while Google Ads modeled many conversions back to ads.
Google Ads can’t use Consent Mode modeling unless analytics_storage is denied too, so the flat Ads line proves consent settings are wrong.
GA4 instantly modeled denied users back to Paid Search, so the drop must be a true performance decline.
concept_mcqs.explanation: With ad_storage denied, ad click identifiers aren’t stored, so GA4 attribution shifts away from Paid Search initially. Google Ads applies consent-mode modeling to recover many conversions to ads, so Ads may look flat while GA4 by-channel looks lower the same day.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Both platforms can model; Ads being flat is expected, not a cache quirk. C: GA4 does model but not necessarily immediately and not identically to Ads; the same-day drop doesn’t prove true decline. D: Consent-mode modeling in Ads does not require denying analytics_storage; this mixes up consent categories.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You reduce the GA4 attribution lookback window from 30 to 7 days. The last 90 days’ time-lag distributions were:

```csv
channel,0-1d,2-7d,8-14d,15-30d
Paid Search,70%,20%,7%,3%
Paid Social,15%,25%,40%,20%
Email,30%,45%,20%,5%
```
Which immediate reporting effect is most likely?
options: Paid Social ROAS drops the most because many conversions now fall outside the 7‑day window.
All channels’ ROAS declines equally because the window change is applied uniformly.
Paid Search ROAS increases because GA4 backfills missing clicks from 8‑14 days into 2‑7 days.
Email ROAS is unaffected; attribution windows don’t apply to owned channels.
concept_mcqs.explanation: With a 7‑day window, Paid Social loses a large 8–14 day tail, so it sees the biggest immediate ROAS drop. Other channels with shorter lags are less affected.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: GA4 doesn’t reclassify 8–14 days into 2–7; those conversions are excluded. C: Lookback windows apply by channel; owned vs paid doesn’t exempt Email. D: Uniform setting, non-uniform effects due to different lag profiles.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your landing URLs contain both auto-tagged `gclid` and manual UTMs:

```text
https://example.com/?gclid=EAIaIQobChMI...&utm_source=google&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=Brand_EMEA
```
The GA4 property is properly linked to Google Ads. What source/medium will GA4 attribution use for the session?
options: google / cpc from the UTM because UTMs always override auto-tagging for transparency.
google / organic because GA4 treats gclid as an organic click ID when UTMs are also present.
google / cpc from the gclid mapping; the manual UTMs are ignored when gclid is present and valid.
(not set) / (not set) because mixed tagging causes GA4 to discard identifiers.
concept_mcqs.explanation: With a valid gclid and a linked Ads account, GA4 uses auto-tagging for source/medium and campaign. Manual UTMs are ignored in this case.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: In Ads-linked properties, gclid takes precedence. C: Mixed tagging doesn’t nullify attribution. D: gclid is paid ads click ID, not organic.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You ran a 50/50 landing page A/B test. Early GA4 Exploration shows:

```csv
variant,sessions,purchases,conversion_rate
A,10000,420,4.20%
B,7800,360,4.62%
```
You expected equal traffic split. What’s the best immediate action regarding budget allocation?
options: Stop the test and keep A because it has more purchases in absolute terms.
Investigate a sample ratio mismatch before reallocating spend; don’t call a winner yet.
Increase total traffic to drown out the imbalance; keep allocating 50/50 in media.
Shift budget to B immediately because its conversion rate is higher despite fewer sessions.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A significant allocation imbalance (SRM) suggests implementation or traffic issues that can bias results. Validate delivery and instrumentation before making budget moves.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Higher CVR can be an artifact of biased assignment. C: Absolute conversions ignore the unequal exposure. D: More traffic doesn’t fix a broken randomization or tracking issue.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You used UTMs like below for Paid Social. Default Channel Grouping rules expect specific mediums (e.g., `paid_social`).

```text
https://example.com/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=paid-social&utm_campaign=Q3_Launch
```
In standard GA4 reports without custom channel definitions, where will most of this traffic land?
options: Referral, because facebook implies referral unless the medium is exactly `cpc`.
Unassigned, because `paid-social` doesn’t match GA4’s Paid Social rules.
Display, because any paid medium defaults to Display when rules don’t match.
Paid Social, because GA4 normalizes hyphens and underscores.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Default Channel Grouping uses strict pattern rules. `paid-social` (with a hyphen) doesn’t match, so traffic often appears as Unassigned unless you define a custom channel rule.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: GA4 doesn’t auto-normalize arbitrary medium values to canonical forms. C: Source alone doesn’t force Referral when UTMs are present. D: There’s no fallback-to-Display rule for unmatched paid mediums.

options: Exclude `begin_checkout` from the revenue aggregation and keep it as a conversion counted without value in ROI tiles.
Turn off `purchase` as a conversion so you only count it once at `begin_checkout`.
Keep both conversions with value and divide total conversion value by two in the dashboard.
Stop sending `value` on `purchase` and keep it only on `begin_checkout`.
concept_mcqs.explanation: For ROI, only revenue-bearing conversions (purchase) should contribute value. Keep `begin_checkout` as a conversion KPI but exclude it from revenue aggregation or don’t send value on it.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Removes true revenue signal. C: Arbitrary halving fails when the mix of conversion types changes. D: Disabling purchase conversion discards your core revenue metric.

concept_mcqs.stem:
While debugging, you spot PII in page URLs sent to GA4:

```http
GET /thank-you?email=anna.sousa%40example.com&order=ORD-55421 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
...
```
What is the realistic outcome and appropriate response?
options: GA4 rejects the entire event when PII is present, so revenue will be missing but policy is safe.
GA4 automatically redacts any email-like query parameters so no action is needed.
Events will be collected and PII may appear in GA4/BigQuery; you must strip PII at collection and file a GA4 data deletion request for affected parameters.
Mark `email` as an event-scoped custom dimension so it’s governed; keeping it avoids policy issues.
concept_mcqs.explanation: GA4 prohibits sending PII but doesn’t guarantee automatic redaction. Such data can be stored and expose compliance risk. The fix is to prevent collection (e.g., strip parameters in GTM/server) and submit a targeted data deletion request.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: There’s no blanket auto-redaction guarantee. C: GA4 does not reliably reject the whole hit. D: Registering a custom dimension compounds the violation; governance doesn’t legitimize PII collection.

scenario_questions.scenario:
Your ecommerce brand runs Paid Search, Paid Social, and Email. The GA4 property uses Data-driven attribution. Last month you used a 30-day lookback. This month, after a finance request to show faster payback, you switched the lookback to 7 days mid-month. Two weeks later, GA4’s Model comparison shows:

- Data-driven vs Cross-channel last click: Paid Social shows a -28% change in conversions; Paid Search shows -3%; Email shows -8%.
- Time lag exploration (last 90 days) indicates Paid Social conversions skew to 8–14 days, Paid Search to 0–1 day, Email to 2–7 days.
- Revenue (server-side) and total GA4 purchases are flat week over week.
Finance is pushing to cut Paid Social budget by 30% immediately based on the GA4 by-channel ROAS trend since the setting change.
scenario_questions.task: Decide whether to cut Paid Social now. Justify your recommendation with attribution mechanics and lag evidence, and propose a measurement plan to validate the decision within two weeks without jeopardizing total revenue.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Do not cut 30% immediately. The observed drop is largely a measurement artifact from shortening the lookback window: Paid Social’s long-lag conversions (8–14 days) now fall outside attribution, depressing its reported ROAS while total purchases are flat. Recommend holding social budget steady or making a small test reduction (e.g., 10%) in a geo-split while monitoring server-side sales and GA4 total purchases. Validate with: (a) compare Data-driven 30-day vs 7-day using the Model comparison over a common historical window; (b) monitor the Time lag report for changes; (c) run a two-week geo lift test or MMM-style pre-post with holdout to estimate incremental ROAS; (d) track KPIs in a dashboard including total purchases, revenue, and blended CAC to prevent false savings. Document the lookback change and annotate reports to prevent misinterpretation.

rubric.criterion: States a clear recommendation on whether to cut budget now (not just analysis)
Cites how lookback window change interacts with long time-lag to depress Paid Social attribution without total sales decline
Proposes a concrete validation plan (e.g., geo-split/holdout or lift test) tied to a two-week horizon
Identifies guardrail metrics (e.g., total purchases/revenue, blended CAC/ROAS) and reporting annotations to avoid misreads

scenario_questions.scenario: Your Google Ads account shows 950 conversions last 7 days for the “Brand_US” campaign. GA4 shows 710 `purchase` conversions attributed to Paid Search for the same period. The property is linked to Ads, GA4 is set to Data-driven attribution, and Consent Mode is on with `ad_storage` denied for about 35% of US users. Auto-tagging is on. Model comparison shows Cross-channel last click is slightly higher for Paid Search than Data-driven. Finance wants to recalibrate ROAS targets downward to match GA4.
scenario_questions.task: Identify the most likely reasons for the discrepancy and list the concrete steps you would take before changing ROAS targets.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Likely causes: (1) Platform scope differences: Ads shows conversions attributed to Ads (including modeled conversions via consent mode), while GA4 Paid Search shows only the portion attributed to that channel under its model; (2) Consent-mode modeling timing/coverage differences cause Ads to recover more conversions to Ads than GA4 attributes to Paid Search; (3) Lookback and attribution model differences (Ads often uses Ads-preferred attribution; GA4 uses cross-channel Data-driven); (4) Reporting identity differences (user vs device) and data thresholds; (5) Import timing and conversion window mismatches. Steps: Verify GA4-to-Ads import status and conversion windows; compare GA4 total purchases vs Paid Search-attributed purchases to isolate attribution vs tracking losses; use the Model comparison report over the same period; check consent diagnostics and the percentage of modeled conversions in Ads; confirm gclid coverage and landing page redirects; ensure currency/time-zone alignment. Only then consider an adjustment, ideally using blended or incrementality-based ROAS benchmarks instead of raw GA4 channel ROAS.

rubric.criterion: Explains at least two attribution/modeling-related causes specific to GA4 vs Ads (not generic ‘tracking error’)
Lists practical verification steps (import status, windows, model comparison, consent diagnostics, gclid coverage)
Advises against immediate target changes and suggests better benchmarking (blended/incremental)

scenario_questions.scenario: After enabling a new checkout, revenue in your GA4 dashboard suddenly inflates by ~20% while server-side orders and revenue remain stable. In GTM, both `begin_checkout` and `purchase` have `value` parameters. The BI team confirms the dashboard sums conversion value across all conversions. You also enabled a new goal to track financing applications (`apply_financing`) and set it as a conversion with a `value` equal to the estimated financed amount.
scenario_questions.task: Diagnose the revenue inflation and specify the changes needed in both GA4 configuration and the dashboard to restore correct ROAS, without losing visibility on `begin_checkout` and `apply_financing`.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The dashboard is double-counting value by summing across conversions, including `begin_checkout` and `apply_financing` values. In GA4, only `purchase` should contribute to revenue for ROAS. Actions: (1) Stop sending `value` on `begin_checkout` (or exclude it from revenue aggregation) and keep it as a conversion KPI; (2) Keep `apply_financing` as a conversion but exclude it from revenue calculations or set its `value` to 0 for ROI views and report it separately as pipeline value; (3) Update the dashboard measure to sum revenue from `purchase` only, or use GA4’s `purchase revenue` metric; (4) Reconcile the last two weeks’ numbers to confirm correction and annotate the change.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the cross-conversion value summation as the cause (begin_checkout and/or apply_financing carrying value)
Recommends GA4-side change to event payloads or conversion settings to prevent value on non-revenue conversions
Specifies dashboard-side metric change to restrict revenue/ROAS to purchase value
Addresses how to retain visibility on non-revenue conversions without polluting ROI (separate tiles or zero-valued KPIs)

scenario_questions.scenario: You must design a two-week headline test for the top Paid Social landing page to improve ROAS. Budget is limited; you can drive ~20,000 sessions over two weeks. Baseline conversion rate is 3.8%. You will measure with GA4 and decide whether to roll out the variant globally or not. Stakeholders want high confidence and a clear stop rule.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a statistically sound test plan: hypothesis, success metric(s), minimum detectable effect, sample size split, guardrails, and a stopping/decision rule. Include how you will instrument and validate the GA4 measurement to avoid SRM or attribution artifacts.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Hypothesis: Variant B’s headline increases purchase conversion rate on Paid Social traffic. Metrics: primary = GA4 purchase conversion rate for the campaign; guardrails = bounce rate/engagement rate, AOV, total purchases. MDE: ~15–20% relative lift (3.8% to ~4.4–4.6%) to be detectable with ~10k sessions per arm over two weeks. Split 50/50 at the ad level, enforce even delivery. Stopping rule: fixed horizon at two weeks unless SRM >2% absolute or early validity fails; use two-proportion z-test or Bayesian credible interval with 95% confidence to declare a winner; otherwise roll to another week or declare inconclusive. Instrumentation: ensure consistent UTMs, remove conflicting on-page redirects, verify gclid/fbclid doesn’t overwrite UTMs; create a GA4 Exploration with experiment_id dimension to track sessions and conversions per arm; monitor for SRM daily; annotate reports. Decision: rollout only if lift >= MDE with guardrails stable; else keep control.

rubric.criterion: States a clear hypothesis and primary success metric aligned to purchase ROAS
Specifies MDE, allocation, and sample size reasoning appropriate for the traffic constraint
Defines guardrails and a concrete stopping/decision rule (confidence/credibility threshold)
Details GA4 instrumentation/validation steps to prevent SRM/attribution issues

practical_tasks.brief: Create a two-week optimization plan that reallocates a fixed budget across Paid Search, Paid Social, and Email, with a testing component and compliance guardrails. Use insights from GA4 measurement to set objectives, forecast ROI, and define reporting.

acceptance_criteria: States measurable objectives (e.g., target ROAS/CAC) mapped to GA4 KPIs.

ROI forecast quality (calculations, assumptions, and week-by-week projections)
